description: We are GraviTEH Not Found, a six-member team joining NASA Space Apps Manila. With experience in climate research, technical work, hackathons, and pitching, we aim to make MODIS and VIIRS fire data easier to compare and understand through maps and a burning activity calendar. We value teamwork, clear communication, and practical solutions to environmental problems. Our team lineup is complete.
summary:
Satellites have tracked global thermal hotspots since 2000, but the record is split across two sensors: MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m resolution). Because VIIRS picks up smaller fires that MODIS misses, raw data shows an artificial jump in 2012, making it difficult for scientists, responders, and land managers to compare long-term fire trends accurately.

To solve this, our machine learning model trains on the 14-year overlap (2012 to 2025) where both sensors operated simultaneously, learning how MODIS detections map to VIIRS sensitivity across different regions and seasons. This allows us to reconstruct VIIRS-equivalent weekly fire activity back to 2000. Burnadette pairs this harmonized dataset with a clean dashboard featuring a 25-year heatmap, seasonal anomaly scoring, and transparent uncertainty intervals, helping decision-makers separate real climate and land-use shifts from sensor artifacts.
details:
Burnadette turns 25 years of raw satellite fire records (2000–2025) into one consistent weekly history across five countries: Belgium, Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Zambia. Instead of counting individual satellite pixels—which differ between old and new sensors—our pipeline maps fires onto a standard grid and measures the share of active squares each week. Using the 14 years when NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites flew together, our model adjusts older MODIS records to match the newer VIIRS sensor, cutting undercounting from up to 72% down to within ±1%. On the website, users pick a region on the map, scan every week on a 25-year heatmap, and click any week to see its fire activity, how unusual it is for that season, whether it was directly observed or estimated, and its confidence range.

By uniting two incompatible satellite records into a single baseline, Burnadette lets emergency responders, climate researchers, and land managers compare modern fire seasons against early-2000s history without being misled by the 2012 sensor upgrade. Our seasonal comparison also spots unusual off-peak fire spikes—such as wet-season agricultural or peatland burning—that would normally get drowned out by dry-season peaks. At the same time, the platform stays transparent about data limits: instead of treating missing data as "zero fires," it flags satellite outages, shows confidence ranges on all pre-2012 estimates, and warns users when small fires (like in Belgium) or heavy cloud cover reduce detection sensitivity.

To build Burnadette, we processed NASA’s open FIRMS satellite fire data using Python (pandas, NumPy, and SciPy) to clean, grid, and calibrate the 25-year dataset. Our backend runs on FastAPI and serves lightweight, pre-compiled JSON files, keeping the system fast and simple without needing a separate cloud database. On the frontend, we built an interactive dashboard with React and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel so users can explore the fire history directly in their browser.
